opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more interesting architectural questions right now. What I'd like to see is less of a world where you have one monolithic model that does everything and a separate fine-tuned copy for every specialty. Instead I'd like something more modular, where you have a really strong general base model that understands language, reasoning, code, images, and so on, and then you can attach specialized pieces of capability to it as needed.

One way to think about it is sparsity. Today's models are already somewhat sparse with mixture-of-experts, but the experts are fairly uniform and learned all at once. I'd love something more organic, where different parts of the model can be developed somewhat independently, and you route to the right components depending on the task. If you're doing something in, say, a particular area of medicine or a specific programming domain, you activate the parts of the model that know about that, plus the general reasoning core, and you don't pay the compute cost of everything else.

That also opens up interesting possibilities for how teams work. Different groups could improve different modules (a better module for some language, or for some scientific field) and contribute them back without having to retrain the whole thing from scratch. You'd want the general model to provide a shared representation space so those pieces compose cleanly, rather than each specialization being an island.

There's a practical side too. Some specialized capabilities depend on data that not everyone should have access to, like private enterprise data or sensitive domains. If you can install a module for a particular customer or use case on top of a shared base, you get the benefits of the general model's broad knowledge while keeping specialized knowledge separate and controllable.

And then there's the tool-use angle, which is complementary. Not every specialized capability needs to live in the weights. Sometimes the right answer is for the general model to be really good at knowing when to call out to a specialized system, whether that's a smaller expert model, a simulator, a search system, or a piece of code, and then integrating the result. So I think the end state is some combination: a general model that's broadly capable, specialized components that can be plugged in efficiently, and good mechanisms for routing and composing all of that. We're not fully there yet, but I think that's the direction that gives you both generality and efficiency.

r001.rationale: It proposes attaching specialized capability modules to a strong general base model and having them compose through a shared representation space.

r002.rationale: It says to route to the right components depending on the task and activate domain-specific parts as needed.

r003.rationale: It mentions medicine as a possible specialty, but does not say healthcare capability should come from large-scale health-data training rather than retrieval.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought a lot about, and I think the way I'd frame it is that we want the model to be more like a modular system than a monolith. Right now, when you train a big dense model, you're kind of doing everything at once. Every parameter gets touched on every example, and if you want to add a new capability, you basically retrain the whole thing or do a big fine-tuning pass that risks disturbing what's already there.

What I'd rather see is something closer to what we sketched out in the Pathways vision a few years ago. You have a general base model that has broad knowledge and strong reasoning, and then you have these specialized pieces, modules or experts or adapters, whatever you want to call them, that can be developed somewhat independently. Maybe one team trains a module that's really good at a particular kind of medical imaging, another trains one that understands a particular codebase or a particular scientific domain, and those can be plugged in without anyone having to redo the base.

The important thing is that the routing between them should be learned, not hand-wired. The model should figure out, for this piece of a problem, I need to pull in this specialized knowledge, and for that piece I can just use the general path. Sparse mixture-of-experts gives you a flavor of this, but today it's mostly about compute efficiency rather than true modularity, since the experts are all trained jointly and you can't really detach one and swap it out. I'd like to push toward a world where you can actually add a new expert to a deployed system, train it on a modest amount of data, and have the rest of the model learn to use it.

There are a couple of practical benefits. One is you can iterate faster on specific capabilities without the cost and risk of touching the whole model. Another is that you can have different update cadences. The base might be refreshed on the scale of months, while a specialized component for, say, a rapidly changing API could be refreshed much more often. And there's a nice story for efficiency too: you only activate the pieces you need, so a system that in total knows an enormous amount only spends compute on the slice relevant to the current task.

The hard research problems are mostly about interfaces. How do you make the representations at the boundary stable enough that a module trained later still speaks the same language as the base? How do you avoid the base model learning to lean on a module in ways that break when you replace it? And how do you get the right kind of credit assignment so that a new module actually gets used when it should be? I don't think we've solved those, but I think it's the direction things need to go if we want systems that keep growing in capability without every improvement requiring a from-scratch effort.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a broad general base model working with independently developed specialized modules that can be plugged in.

r002.rationale: It says learned routing should select specialized knowledge for the relevant part of a problem and use the general path elsewhere.

r003.rationale: It mentions a medical imaging module trained on some data, but does not suggest that healthcare capability should come from large-scale health-data training rather than retrieval.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to have a fairly general model that understands enough about a wide variety of things to know when it needs some more specialized help. Then, depending on the problem, it could bring in the right capabilities—maybe a model that’s particularly good at some scientific domain, or a tool that can execute code—and incorporate those results into what it’s doing.

The interesting challenge is learning how to make those decisions. Which capabilities should you use for this input? How much computation should you spend? You don’t want to activate everything for every question. You want the system to draw on the right expertise, and perhaps combine several kinds of expertise when the problem requires it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a general model bringing in specialized models or tools and incorporating their results.

r002.rationale: It says the system should select capabilities depending on the problem and use the right expertise for the input.

r003.rationale: The candidate mentions scientific-domain models and code-execution tools, but says nothing about healthcare, health-data training, or retrieval.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like to see a general model that’s very capable on its own, but also knows when to draw on more specialized expertise. You might have a component that’s particularly good at mathematics, another at writing code, and another that understands a particular scientific domain. The general model could figure out which capabilities are useful for a given problem and bring them together.

The interesting challenge is how you train that whole system so the pieces cooperate effectively. You want specialization without having to activate every capability for every request. Ideally, a simple question takes very little computation, while a difficult problem can draw on more expertise and spend more time working through it.

r001.rationale: It describes a capable general model bringing together specialized capabilities, such as mathematics, coding, and scientific expertise.

r002.rationale: It says the general model should determine which capabilities are useful for a given problem and invoke them accordingly.

r003.rationale: It mentions no healthcare specialization, health data, or training approach.
